text.p: Current average ex-Hong Kong air cargo market rates in Hong Kong dollars per kg for a 100kg shipment, with volume-to-weight of six to one.
Jan 10 Dec 11
EUROPE
MIDDLE EAST
* The rates quoted in this report were obtained by Reuters journalists on a confidential basis from a range of airliners, large forwarders and smaller air cargo agents.
* All prices quoted in Hong Kong dollars.
* The tariffs represent average rates calculated from a range of prices and are indicative of current market activity.
HK air cargo market await pre-Chines New Year surge
By Jim Gilchrist

HONG KONG, Jan 10 (Reuter) - Hong Kong's air cargo industry is recovering from a frenetic Christmas peak season which observers said was the busiest for years and is anticipating another surge in the run-up to the Chinese New Year in early February, a Reuters survey showed.

With the first week in January traditionally one of the quietest periods of the year, major cargo carrying airlines such as Lufthansa Cargo, Cathay Pacific and KLM are all reporting unusually heavy demand.

For many other airlines and freight forwarders it's a case of catching their breath before what they hope is a profitable surge before the Chinese new year holiday when the territory comes to a virtual standstill and factories in China shut down for two weeks.
A major talking point has been a rise on ex-Hong Kong rates to Europe which has largely replaced a controversial fuel surcharge imposed by some carriers before Christmas.

Almost all the major carriers to Europe have taken advantage of the stronger than normal market to raise their ex-Hong Kong market rate by up to HK$1.80. Many agreed to withdraw the 80 cents a kilo fuel surcharge before the year end and raise rates instead.

From January 1, most carriers had raised their market rates by another HK$1 above the surcharge level. Hong Kong's home carrier Cathay Pacific, which did not impose a fuel surcharge raised its rate by HK$1.50.

As one airline manager admitted the whole question of a fuel surcharge is "a very touchy subject" which has angered freight forwarders who complain of four ex-Hong Kong rate rises since September. Airline managers, struggling as ever to gain yield, insist rates are still lower now than they were three years ago.

"What the airlines are doing is making a rate increase, but making it more palatable by taking away the fuel surcharge. From the forwarders point of view that's not particularly clever. Most have big contracts offering a year round rate and we have to absorb any increase. With a fuel surcharge you can pass that straight on to the customer, but with a rate increase you can't," one leading freight forwarder complained.
In reply, one leading airline's cargo manager said if the airlines raise rates by one dollar, freight forwarders raise by two "so make no mistake they are making money."

Sam Chung, chairman of the Hong Kong Association of Freight Forwarding Agents, said rates were, surprisingly, rising as the market was falling as airlines apparently anticipate another surge leading up to Chinese new year.

"The rate increase by all carriers to Europe was unexpected because normally when the market slows down, rates should come down too. I think European carriers are looking forward to Chinese New year and they figure the market will pick up before the holiday. Normally there is a rush in all markets leading up to Chinese new year. After the new year holiday, I think rates will come down.
"The fuel surcharge which we thought was illegal has gone and the airlines have raised their rates instead which we can't argue about, Chung stated."
Tom Presnail, regional director sales for KLM Cargo in North Asia said the Hong Kong market was still remarkably strong.
"After minimum disruption at Christmas our planes are full again. We are extremely pleased with how things have been going", he said.

Lufthansa agreed. "The beginning of January is normally very poor but we still have full flights. In fact the demand is too high and we have had to off load some cargo. The demand will increase up to Chinese New Year when everyone rushes to get their goods out before they go on holiday," said a Lufthansa Cargo spokesman.

Lufthansa had refused to withdraw its fuel surcharge, instead raising its market rate by HK$1 from January 1 and is maintaining a separate 80 cents fuel surcharge imposed before Christmas, an airline source said.
KLM said it raised ex-Hong Kong market rates on December 16 by 80 Hong Kong cents a kilo in response to rising fuel prices and may raise rates again in the near future.
"We are considering raising rates by five to ten per cent within this first quarter but the size of the rise will depend on local circumstances," Presnail said.
Air France Cargo regional manager Philippe Bour has ruled out further rate rises after it raised its market rate by HK$1 from January 1 and decided to continue with an 80 HK cents fuel surcharge.
He said early January had been quiet with several freighter flights being cancelled but is optimistic of another busy period ahead.

"At the moment it is very quiet and I've cancelled two flights this week but I am hopeful for the coming weeks and the 15 days before Chinese new year are usually very strong. However forwarders were very optimistic last year and there was a very weak market so we will have to wait and see," Bour said.
Emirates was also hopeful of another busy period before Chinese New Year.
"After the Christmas holiday things slowed down a bit but we expect it to pick up after this weekend. We presume the market will boom up to Chinese new year," a spokesman said.

The Dubai based carrier, which has seven passenger flights a week from Hong Kong to Dubai plus two freighter flights wet leased from Atlas Air, had been charging a fuel surcharge during December. But that was stopped on January 1 and rates raised instead by 80 cents a kilo to Middle East destinations and by HK$1.80 to European destinations, a spokesman said.

"We have informed our customers and contract agents that we will maintain the surcharge of 80 cents and raise our rates by (an additional) HK$1. Compared to December they will be paying a dollar extra because the 80 cents surcharge is now embedded in the rate. We are still convinced that a fuel surcharge is the best way and fairer but that is what we have now done," said an Emirates spokesman.

In contrast, British Airways, a major cargo carrying player with twice daily passenger flights to Heathrow and dedicated freighter flights to London Gatwick, is adopting a 'wait and see' approach to any cargo rate increase.

"I'm not commenting yet about any price increase. At the moment we are reserving our judgement and waiting to see how we come back after Christmas. But the market is still very very buoyant and looks very favourable in terms of supply and demand." said BA's regional cargo manager for the Pacific region, Chris Humphrey.
A BA rate rise is anticipated by the rest of the industry.
As one cargo manager put it: "If some airlines don't raise their rates they will be missing out."
BA last raised market rates ex-Hong Kong before Christmas taking advantage of strong market demand. Humphrey was optimistic about future prospects.

"There was a slight dip over Christmas week, which you'd expect but last week's figures were impressive. We expect our freight business to remain buoyant until Chinese New Year. It looks a very positive outlook for the next month which we are obviously pleased about," Humphrey said.

A spokesman for Alitalia, which increased its rate on January the first by HK$1.80 per kilo, said he had been happy with business since September enjoying 90 per cent load factors on its weekly Boeing 747 freighter flight to Milan and Rome. The Italian flag carrier also operates three passenger flights a week direct to Rome.

Virgin Atlantic was another European carrier to raise its rate on January 1. A spokesman for Virgin's Hong Kong cargo agent said there had been a noticeable drop in demand after New Year, possibly because shippers were awaiting new export licences from the Hong Kong and Chinese governments. Until that happens goods are being stored, he said.

Industry sources said so-called second tier, indirect carriers which serve European destinations via an Asia hub, such as Singapore Airlines and Thai Airways International, were offering rates to Europe between HK$15 to 18.
That compares with major direct carriers to Europe such as Lufthansa Cargo which is taking advantage of high demand and is able to charge HK$25 a kilo on faster, direct services to Frankfurt.

Some freight forwarders said demand for space has been made more difficult with the cancellation of flights. Lufthansa Cargo said it had two fewer flights in early January because aircraft were undergoing maintenance at what is usually a quiet time of the year.
Inter-Asian market prices are said to be holding firm.

Observers said the pre-Christmas peak period was the busiest in Hong Kong for many years. Hong Kong Air Cargo Terminals Limited (HACTL), which enjoys a monopoly on all air cargo handling, said it set a series of new daily, weekly and monthly import handling records during December.

"Imports remain strong, especially shipments destined for Hong Kong's new airport at Chek Lap Kok where contractors face tight deadlines to complete projects," said HACTL managing director Anthony Charter.
Bryan Chan, Hong Kong general manager for TNT Express Worldwide (HK) Ltd, said the express market is much healthier than general freight market.

"The entire air cargo industry is having a boom but average growth for the express industry is easily well over 20 per cent. TNT's document, parcel and express freight business in Hong Kong is exceeding 30 per cent annual growth.
In general the outlook appears favourable for good business over the coming weeks but rates are forecast to drop after Chinese new year and stay flat until August or September.

As one freight forwarder put it: "We're having a brief respite before another big rush up to Chinese new year. Then we should have a few days rest before another rush towards Easter. The prospects are good," he said. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
